title: The Priest of God Most High Came Out to Meet Him — Sword, Bread, a Tenth
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Last lesson we watched Abram hand the best piece of land over to his nephew. Lot lifted up his eyes, chose the whole plain of the Jordan, travelled east — and then, little by little, moved his tent as far as Sodom.

The question this lesson puts to us is one that every elder, every parent, everyone who has ever led another person has run into: once you and someone have gone your separate ways — once the household has been divided — how far are you still responsible for him?

By any ordinary human reckoning, Abram could have said: he chose this road himself, and I warned him long ago. But in chapter 14, the moment he hears that his nephew has been carried off, he leads out three hundred and eighteen men from his own household and pursues them through the night, for hundreds of kilometres.

Let me put the answer up front: letting go is not the same as giving up. You can lay down your control over a person without laying down your love for him. And the one sentence a person who has truly won most needs to hear is this — that was God's doing.
1. One Tent in the Middle of International Politics
Verse 1: "In the days of Amraphel, king of Shinar; Arioch, king of Ellasar; Chedorlaomer, king of Elam; and Tidal, king of Goiim …"

Brothers and sisters, this run of names is hard to pronounce, but I want you to notice the very first place-name: Shinar, שִׁנְעָר (*Shin'ar*). You have met it before, in chapter 11 — that is the plain where they built the tower of Babel. The power of Babel is back, and this time it comes with an army.

Verse 2 says, "they made war with Bera, king of Sodom; Birsha, king of Gomorrah …", and verse 4 says that these five kings "served Chedorlaomer for twelve years, and in the thirteenth year they rebelled."

Brothers and sisters, this is the first time the word "war", מִלְחָמָה (*milchamah*), appears in Genesis. The first war in the Bible is recorded right here, and what set it off was tribute and rebellion — which is to say, money and power.

And why does the author spend twelve whole verses on an international war that has nothing to do with Abram? Because he wants you to see one thing: this man who has been called does not live in a vacuum. He lives in a tent, he builds altars, he pastures sheep — but the world he lives in has four kings and five kings in it, and tribute, and rebellion, and refugees.

Verse 10 hides a detail worth stopping for: "Now the valley of Siddim was full of tar pits". The Hebrew is בֶּאֱרֹת בֶּאֱרֹת חֵמָר — pit after pit of bitumen. And חֵמָר (*chemar*) is precisely the tar they used in chapter 11, verse 3, to build the tower of Babel. Brothers and sisters, the very material once used to raise a tower has become the pit the kings fall into. What people use to climb higher very often turns, in the end, into the hole they trip in.

Verse 12: "They took Lot, Abram's brother's son, who lived in Sodom, and his goods, and departed." Watch the progression. Genesis 13:12 said he "moved his tent as far as Sodom"; Genesis 14:12 says he "lived in Sodom". The end of moving your tent a little at a time is that one day your name is on the household register there.
Abram took over three hundred men out to fight. Are Christians allowed to use force?

This passage is narrative, not command, so it cannot be picked up and used as a licence for force. What we can say for certain is this: Abram did not go out to expand his territory, he went to rescue a kinsman who had been carried off; and when the rescue was over he handed back every person and every article of property, keeping nothing at all. In other words, this was a rescue, not a conquest. As for the wider question of Christians and force, church history holds several positions — absolute pacifism, just war theory, and self-defence under lawful authority. These study notes will not settle any of them from the pulpit, but there is one line we must hold: Scripture may never be used to justify hatred, revenge or vigilante violence. What is worth learning from this chapter is his motive — he went to save a person, not to collect spoil.
"He heard, and he went" — does rescuing someone always have to be that fast? I usually need time to think things over.

Some things need thinking over; with other things, by the time you have thought them over it is already too late. The way to tell them apart is to ask: if this drags on, who pays the price? If the price falls on you, take your time. If the price falls on somebody else, move quickly. Abram's situation was perfectly clear — Lot had been carried off, and every hour of delay made it more dangerous. And notice that he was not being impulsive. The men he led out were his "three hundred eighteen trained men, born in his house" — men trained long before the emergency ever came. He divided his forces, struck by night, pursued as far as Dan: it was all done by the book. So fast does not mean reckless. What actually makes a person able to move fast is having been made ready beforehand.
Verse 13: "One who had escaped came and told Abram, the Hebrew."

Brothers and sisters, this is the first time in the Bible that the name "Hebrew", הָעִבְרִי (*ha'Ivri*), appears. The root of the word means "to cross over" — the one who came across the river. In other people's eyes he was an outsider, a man who had crossed over from the far side.
Verse 14: "When Abram heard that his relative was taken captive, he led out his three hundred eighteen trained men, born in his house, and pursued as far as Dan."

Notice those words, "his relative." Both verse 12 and verse 14 go out of their way to name the family tie. The author wants you to remember it: that is his nephew — the nephew who picked out the best piece of land for himself, the nephew who moved into Sodom.
And Abram's response costs the text almost no words at all: he heard, and he went. No meeting. No assessment. Not one syllable of "I told him so."

Brothers and sisters, this is a very hard thing. The hardest step in forgiveness is not letting go of the grudge inside; it is getting to your feet when the other person is in trouble. You can talk yourself into "I have forgiven him already" — but the real test lies here: when the person who wronged you gets into trouble, do you move or not?

Verse 15 says he "divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them." Three hundred and eighteen herdsmen against a coalition of four kings who had just beaten a coalition of five — and he does it at night, in divided companies. This battle was fought by a professional. Then verse 16: "He brought back all the goods, and also brought back his relative Lot and his goods, and the women also, and the other people."
Everything recovered, nothing left behind. And when the fighting was over, he did not ask for a single inch of ground.
Who is Melchizedek? Where does his importance actually lie?

He occupies three verses of Genesis and no more, and yet he is one of the most intriguing figures in the whole Old Testament. The text calls him "king of Salem" and also "priest of God Most High" — king and priest in one person, two offices that Israel's later system kept strictly apart. Psalm 110:4 says, "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek"; and Hebrews spends the whole of chapter 7 explaining him: without father, without mother, without genealogy, no record of his birth and none of his death, and so he becomes a type of the one who is priest for ever. He matters not because there is anything mysterious about him in himself, but because he points to that one. So when you preach him, the last picture must come to rest on Christ, and not stop at guesswork.
"He brought out bread and wine" — is this a foreshadowing of the Lord's Supper?

Interpreters down the centuries have mostly seen the echo here — bread and wine, a priest, a blessing, all of which turn up again at the Last Supper. But two things need saying plainly. First, Genesis itself never explains the scene as the Lord's Supper, so what we are speaking of is a type and an echo; we are not saying that Melchizedek was celebrating communion. Second, the reason the echo carries any weight at all is that the New Testament itself picks up the line — Hebrews is the book that ties him to Christ. So the echo may certainly be preached, but say "this makes us think of" and not "this is." Keep that proportion and what the congregation takes home is a method for reading Scripture, and not merely a pretty association.
3. A Light from the Original: Bread, Wine, and God Most High
Verse 17: "The king of Sodom went out to meet him after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, at the valley of Shaveh (that is, the King's Valley)."

Brothers and sisters, notice that two kings come out at the same moment to meet one man fresh from a victory. And the author's arrangement is beautifully done: he brings the king of Sodom out first, then cuts the camera away and inserts the three verses about Melchizedek, and only afterwards comes back to let the king of Sodom speak. This is a sandwich structure — and in a sandwich structure, the filling in the middle is the point.
Verse 18: "Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine. He was priest of God Most High."

"Melchizedek", מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק (*Malki-tzedek*), means "my king is righteousness"; and "Salem", שָׁלֵם (*shalem*), is peace — the city that later becomes Jerusalem. So Hebrews 7:2 says that he is "first, by interpretation, 'king of righteousness', and then also 'king of Salem', which means 'king of peace'."

And what he brings out is bread and wine. Brothers and sisters, this is the first time in the Bible that those two things are set side by side. Thousands of years later, in an upper room in Jerusalem, the Lord Jesus took bread and gave thanks, and then he took the cup — the same city, and the same two things.

In verse 19 he says, "Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth." "God Most High" is אֵל עֶלְיוֹן (*El Elyon*). And here is what is interesting: that title existed inside Canaanite religion as well. So when Abram answers in verse 22, he does something very important. He says, "I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth" — he accepts the title, and he sets the name of Yahweh in front of it.

Brothers and sisters, that is a whole lesson in evangelism. He does not throw out every word the other man uses. He starts from the word the other man already understands, and then he adds the name of God to it. Paul did exactly the same thing in Athens — he saw the altar inscribed "TO AN UNKNOWN GOD" and said, "What therefore you worship in ignorance, I announce to you."

Verse 20: "Abram gave him a tenth of all." Notice this: it happens four hundred years before the law, and nobody had laid down a rule requiring it of him. This is not a regulation. It is the voluntary response of a man who has just been given a victory.
The tenth was there before the law was ever handed down. How should we think about giving today, then?

That is exactly the point worth noticing: Abram gave his tenth four hundred years before the law of Moses. So the root of tithing is not a legal requirement; it is the natural response of a man who has been blessed. The New Testament never restates the ten-per-cent figure, but it pushes the standard deeper still: "Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." So healthy teaching runs like this: do not use the tithe to tie up anybody's conscience, and do not use "New Testament freedom" as an excuse for giving nothing. The practical way to do it is to settle on a proportion, give it regularly, and let it be joyful rather than fearful.
Then the camera returns to the king of Sodom. Verse 21: "The king of Sodom said to Abram, 'Give me the people, and take the goods for yourself.'"

This is an extremely generous offer. By the customs of war in that world, everything recovered belonged to the overcomer by right in any case; the king of Sodom is in effect speaking first in order to hand the property over.

And Abram's answer is the loveliest thing in the chapter: "I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours, lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'"
Brothers and sisters, notice two things here.

The first: he says, "I have lifted up my hand" — the thing was already done. It was not something that occurred to him on the spot, standing in front of the king of Sodom. Before the battle, before he had laid eyes on that heap of plunder, he had already drawn the line in God's presence. And that is the most practical lesson this whole chapter gives us — you will not find the strength to refuse in the moment the temptation arrives. You find it because you decided before anything happened.

The second: the reason he gives for refusing is "lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'" He will not let a king of Sodom put his signature on his blessing. Brothers and sisters, the single thread most likely to tie up a person's service is the question of who gave it to him. If what you enjoy today gives somebody the right to say to you, "Don't forget who it came from", then sooner or later that thread will be pulled tight.

And notice how sharply he distinguishes: a tenth to the priest of God Most High, and not one thread from the king of Sodom. In a single afternoon he receives from one hand and refuses the other. What comes from God he takes; what comes with a price tag he does not.

And verse 24 must not be left out: "I will accept nothing from you except that which the young men have eaten, and the portion of the men who went with me: Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their portion." Brothers and sisters, he set a high standard for himself and did not make the decision on anyone else's behalf. That one sentence has saved a great many spiritual leaders — you may refuse for yourself, but you may not fasten your own high standard onto somebody else.
"I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap nor anything that is yours" — is that kind of insistence not rather inhuman?

His reason is stated perfectly clearly: "lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'" It is not that he had no need of it. It is that he would not give anyone the chance to write God's blessing into his own accounts. That is a very high degree of self-awareness, and it is also an intensely practical protection — a man who has accepted favours from the king of Sodom will find it very hard, afterwards, to tell Sodom the truth. For anyone in service today that is immediately practical: whose money you have taken and whose favours you owe will decide how hard it becomes to be honest with him later. Of course this does not mean you may never accept any help at all — he accepted Melchizedek's bread and wine. The discernment lies here: will this gift tie me up, so that later on I dare not say the thing I ought to say?
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching Melchizedek as a mysterious figure who came down out of heaven. Hebrews 7:3 says he was "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life", and some have argued from that verse that he simply is the pre-incarnate Christ. But notice how the same verse goes on: he was "made like the Son of God" — and whatever is made like someone is not that someone. And in ancient usage "without father, without mother, without genealogy" means "not recorded", not "did not in fact have any." He was a real king who was also a priest, appointed by God as a type of Christ. Preach him as a riddle and the congregation's attention slides off Christ and onto textual detective work.

The second is using this chapter to build the formula "give a tenth and get a blessing." Abram gave willingly after the victory; he did not give first in order to ask afterwards. And what he gave was war spoil, not his annual income. Preach it as a transaction and giving turns into investment, and the congregation's motive for giving shifts from gratitude to the expectation of a return. What this verse establishes is the order of giving God the first portion — not a rate of taxation.

The third is preaching "not even a thread" as though Christians may never accept a gift of any kind. In verse 24 he says explicitly that the young men and the men who went with him may take the portion due to them. He refused his own share; he did not refuse on anybody else's behalf. And Paul, in Philippians 4, gladly received the support the church at Philippi sent him. The point of discernment is this: does the gift give the giver authority over you?

The fourth is preaching this war as encouragement for Christians to be combative. Abram marched out to rescue a man, not to enlarge his holdings, and afterwards he did not want a single inch of ground. If you do not say so plainly, this chapter is very easily used to justify a fight, and even to put a blessing on somebody's war. When the congregation has heard you, they should be more willing to stand up for a person, not more eager to win.

The fifth is preaching "three hundred and eighteen men beat four kings" as a spiritual formula for guaranteed victory. The text says he "divided himself against them by night" — that is tactics. The text also says that God Most High "has delivered your enemies into your hand" — that is sovereignty. Both are true. Preach the miracle without the preparation and the congregation learns not to do its part; preach the tactics without the sovereignty and you have delivered a lecture on management.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: there is a relative in my family who keeps getting into trouble, and I have bailed him out many times — how much longer am I supposed to keep rescuing him? Brothers and sisters, this is one of the truest pains in Chinese family life. Let me offer three distinctions. First, saving a life and paying a bill are not the same thing. What Abram went out to rescue was a life that had been carried off; he did not go and settle a gambling debt for Lot. When a person's life is in danger, that is unconditional. When a person keeps asking you to carry the consequences of his own choices, that is another matter altogether — Proverbs 19:19 says, "A hot-tempered man must pay the penalty, for if you rescue him, you must do it again." Scripture itself says "you must do it again", and that is a very clear-eyed sentence. Second, once the rescue was over, Abram did not keep Lot at his side. He sent him back, let him return to the place he had chosen for himself, and go on bearing his own choices. Letting go is not giving up — but neither is it taking over. Third, rescuing someone does not mean rescuing him on his terms. You are allowed to choose how you help: buying him a meal, yes; handing him cash, not necessarily; going with him to the hospital, yes; lying to his boss for him, no.

The second question: Chinese people take the debt of favour very seriously. Once you have accepted somebody's kindness you owe him, and when he later asks you to do something you should not do, refusing is very hard. What help does this chapter give? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives an intensely practical answer, and it is that one sentence: "I have lifted up my hand." Everything turns on the timing — he decided before he had ever laid eyes on the property. So the real homework is not learning how to refuse. It is learning how to decide in advance. You can draw the lines today, on a few specific matters: what kind of money I will not take, what kind of dinner invitation I will not attend, what kind of favour I will not owe. Judge it only once the moment arrives and your judgement will be held hostage by the pressure of that moment. And notice the reason Abram gives — he does not say "I don't need it." He says, "lest you should say, 'I have made Abram rich.'" He puts the reason on God's reputation rather than on his own high-mindedness. Put that way, the other man is also far less likely to feel insulted.
If I refuse the grey-area benefits at work, will I still be able to carry on doing the job at all?

This is exactly the tension this section has to face, and there is no need to pretend that it costs nothing. Three practical steps. First, write your own lines down, and write them down before anything happens; work it out on the spot and you will usually compromise. Second, let systems protect you: where there is a company process to go through, go through the process, and do not rely on a private understanding between two people. Third, find a spiritual companion who knows where your lines are, and give him the right to ask you. As for the cost, be honest that there really will be one — it may be a slower promotion, or fewer contracts coming your way. But remember the reason Abram gave: what he was protecting was not an unblemished image, it was the freedom to tell the truth later on. That freedom is worth that price.
7. Living 321 Out — One Hand Receiving the Blessing, One Hand Offering It Up
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Melchizedek came out carrying bread and wine, and Psalm 110:4 says, "You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." Hebrews spends two whole chapters explaining what that means. Brothers and sisters, a priest does two things: he hands God's blessing to people, and he carries people's thanks up to God. And the Lord Jesus did both — he took the bread and the cup in the upper room, and he offered himself up on the cross. My role model is this: one hand passing the blessing on to people, and one hand returning the thanks to God.

The Bible is my standard — this chapter lets us see that a standard is something that can be settled in advance. "I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High" — the power of that sentence lies in its tense. It was already done. A standard is not a reference book you go and consult once the trouble has arrived; it is something that has been living inside you since before the trouble came.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice how fine Abram's discernment is here: the same afternoon, two kings, two entirely different responses. Discernment like that does not come from cleverness. It comes from a heart that was aligned long beforehand. 1 Corinthians 2:15 says, "But he who is spiritual discerns all things." That discerning is not foreknowledge. It is the ability to tell one thing from another.

Let Jesus be King — "I have lifted up my hand to Yahweh, God Most High" is itself a declaration about sovereignty. He took a matter that had not yet happened and settled it in God's presence beforehand. To let Jesus be King is to draw the line in front of him before the thing ever happens.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — Melchizedek's blessing comes in two halves: "Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth", and then "Blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand." Brothers and sisters, the second half is exactly what a man fresh from a victory most needs to hear — that was God's doing. The thirty minutes after a victory are when pride finds it easiest to walk in.

Establish God's system — the tenth turns up four hundred years before the law, and it is given freely. That tells us one thing: the source of giving is not regulation, it is response. To establish God's system is to set the first portion apart as holy before anything else is done with it — not waiting for a rule to require it, but deciding it for yourself first.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about denying of self and about not living for ourselves, and Abram in this chapter really did not take a single thread. But notice the balance in verse 24: he did not decide on behalf of his servants and his allies. If we turn a personal high standard into a requirement laid on the group, that is not denying of self at all — that is controlling people in the name of denying of self. In a healthy system the leader is strict with himself and generous with everybody else. In an unhealthy one it is precisely the other way round.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One and the Same Victory
Brothers and sisters, one and the same victory falls into four different kinds of heart — and what grows out of it is completely different in each.

When the proud heart has won the battle, its first thought is, "I said all along that he would come to grief." This heart smuggles a comment in along with the rescue, and keeps a piece of leverage in reserve along with the help. Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end the text never records Abram saying one word to Lot. He rescued him, and then he let him go back. Real help comes with no humiliation attached.

The fearful heart says, "Three hundred and eighteen men — how could they possibly win?" When this heart meets something beyond its own capacity, its first reaction is to add up the odds. And to a heart like that I want to say: Abram really did do the arithmetic — the text says plainly that he divided his forces and struck at night; he used his head. But the reason he went was not that the numbers came out in his favour. The reason he went was that it was his nephew. Some things you do not do because you are sure of the outcome. You do them because they are right.

The ashamed heart says, "Somebody like me — who am I to go and rescue anyone?" You may feel that you are a mess, that you cannot even keep your own days in order. Brothers and sisters, notice that Abram had only just come back from Egypt in disgrace one chapter earlier, having lied and been rebuked for it by a foreign king. God did not wait until he had turned into a perfect man before using him. You do not have to repair yourself first in order to hold somebody else up.

The wounded heart says, "He took the best of it back then. On what grounds am I now supposed to go and rescue him?" Brothers and sisters, that sentence is entirely reasonable, and I have no intention of denying that you were wronged. I only want to ask you to look at one thing. When Abram went out to rescue him, Lot had not apologised, and the text records no word of thanks from Lot afterwards either. There is no scene of reconciliation anywhere in this chapter. So what the chapter is saying is not "he changed, and therefore he was worth rescuing." It is saying, "he is my nephew." And if you cannot do it yet, that is all right — let God heal that wound first; you do not have to force yourself to march out before he has.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, draw a line in advance. This week write down three things you decide beforehand that you will not do: one kind of money you will not take, one kind of occasion you will not attend, one kind of thing you will not say. Write them down, and say them once in God's presence. Abram's strength came from that sentence, "I have lifted up my hand."

Second, do one concrete thing for someone who once wronged you. It does not have to be large — a phone call, one time of praying for him, one specific piece of help. The test of forgiveness is not inside your heart. It is whether your feet move in that direction.

Third, give the glory first after a victory. If something comes off for you this week, then before you tell a single person, spend three minutes telling God: this was your doing. Melchizedek's blessing was prepared for the thirty minutes that follow a victory.

Fourth, check the threads of obligation you are carrying. Is there anyone from whom you have accepted a favour that now keeps you from telling the truth about certain things? Take that matter into prayer and look at how it ought to be dealt with.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences. There is a man in the Bible whose nephew took the best piece of land from him; later that nephew was carried off, and the moment he heard of it he took his men out through the night to rescue him. After the rescue somebody offered him the spoil, and he said, "I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap, lest you should say that you made me rich." And so I learned two things — letting go is not giving up, and the line has to be drawn before anything happens.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I may stop managing how he chooses, but I cannot stop caring whether he lives or dies.
I declare that I will draw my lines in God's presence before the thing ever arrives.
I declare that I will let no one put his signature on my blessing; what I have comes from God.
I declare that after a victory I will first say "this was God's doing", and only then say anything else.
This week I am supposed to move once for somebody else's trouble — but I have helped people before and been taken advantage of. What then?

Being used is a real experience; there is no need to deny it, and no need to vow never to help again because of it. This chapter offers two balancing points. First, the person Abram rescued was somebody with a clear relationship to him and a clear need — he did not go out for every single person who opened his mouth. So help may have a boundary drawn round it, and that is not coldness, it is responsibility. Second, once the rescue was over he came home; he did not bring Lot back to live with him. A rescue is not the same thing as long-term carrying. Practically, then: give one piece of help that is concrete, that has an end to it, and that is within your power; do not hand out a promise you cannot afford to keep. And if the other person crosses the line again and again, you may stop, and say clearly where the line is.
Brothers and sisters, if only one picture from this lesson may remain, I want it to be the priest walking out with bread and wine.

Here is a man just come from a battle, covered in dust, the sword still in his hand, the rescued people and the recovered goods following on behind him. He is about to face a king carrying a purse. And before that happens, a priest comes out to him first, bringing bread and wine, and says two things: blessed be you of God Most High; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered your enemies into your hand.

Brothers and sisters, the order of those two sentences matters. First "God has blessed you", and then "it was God who did it." Grace comes first and the glory afterwards. And it was only after Abram had heard both of them that he had the strength to say to the king of Sodom, "I will not take a thread."
You have to be blessed first before you are able to refuse. A person who is empty inside finds it very hard to turn down what is being held out to him.

And Hebrews 7 tells us that this priesthood was made "not after the law of a fleshly commandment, but after the power of an endless life", and that he "lives forever to make intercession for them." Brothers and sisters, you have a high priest today, and his term of office is for ever. At that junction where you have just finished a battle, filthy and worn out and about to face a temptation, he is waiting for you with bread and wine.

The focus is not on whom I rescued, not on what I refused, and not on how handsomely I fought this particular battle. The focus is on Jesus — he is the Lord who is a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to get to our feet when the other person is in trouble, and to draw the line before the spoil is ever piled up in front of us. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ Abram "heard, and he went" — and yet he was not reckless. Fast without being reckless: what does that rest on?
2. ★★★ "I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap" — what was he actually protecting? How does that apply today?
3. ★ Melchizedek came out with bread and wine, and blessed him. What does that picture remind you of?
4. ★★ The tenth came four hundred years before the law. How does that change your understanding of giving?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I helped him; he ought to remember it), fearful (I am afraid of getting myself into trouble), ashamed (I once took something I should not have taken), wounded (someone I helped turned round and bit me). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Blessed be Abram of God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?

7. ★★ Is there a benefit or a favour in your hands that, once taken, makes it hard for you to speak freely? You do not have to give the details. Only say this: what is the sentence it keeps you from saying?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I am most likely to turn a blind eye to is …"
9. ★★ This week, which line drawn in advance are you going to write down for yourself? Say it out loud.

Leader's reminder: question nine will touch the grey areas of the workplace. Do not press for details, and do not let the group pass comment on any company or any person. If anything unlawful is involved, encourage him to seek the formal channels and professional advice.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own extended family, is there someone this week you ought to go to the moment you hear? Say his name, and say what you are going to do.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work or at school, who is currently being given a hard time?
12. ★★★ The practice of giving first: this week, regularly set apart a proportion of your income or your time and offer it up before anything else is spent. Say the proportion, and say the slot.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the line you have written down, and give him the right to ask you about it at any time. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, there is a man in the Bible who won the battle and would not take so much as a sandal strap. Second, his reason was that he would not have anyone able to say, "I am the one who made him rich." Third, so I learned that some benefits are refused in order to keep the freedom to tell the truth later on. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one line you are going to write down this week, and the one person you are going to help. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep our hands clean and to keep our hearts from growing cold.
